Welcome to Chairs

You are looking at the whole training programme in one place: six modules, 105 slides, covering the Rules of Procedure, Effective Communication, Design Thinking, Entrepreneurship & Innovation, the Major Events that shaped the world you will debate, and how to research a company portfolio to primary-source standard.

Two things worth knowing before you start. First, every line is tagged with where it came from: a crimson tag means it traces to a Diplomathon document at the page named, and in Module 1 those are binding rules. A green tag means it is added teaching, useful but not procedure. You should always be able to tell the difference between what the rules say and what anyone, including me, thinks about them.

Second, this is built to be revised alone, not only watched once:

  • Your place is saved. Close the tab and it offers to bring you back.
  • It works offline after your first visit.
  • / searches all 105 slides.
  • M jumps between modules.
  • T changes theme, F goes fullscreen.
  • Any slide is linkable: send a classmate the URL.

The committee rewards the delegate who can make a claim, name its source, propose an action, and defend all three under challenge. Everything here is aimed at that.

          Six modules, one committee

          Each module is its own session. They are not independent: every later module feeds the speech you give under the rules taught in Module 1.

          The research spine ROP p.3 md §2

          One five-step spine runs through every module

          The Rules of Procedure name five research points. Every other module is a way of doing one of them better.

          1. Portfolio. Who you are: Country, Character or CompanyModule 6 covers the Company case in full
          2. Committee: the organisation you represent that portfolio inWhat it regulates, and why your portfolio sits in the room
          3. Agenda: past of the agenda, and current situation of the agendaModule 5 supplies the historical half of this
          4. Policy stance: PEST analysis against the comparators that matterModule 3 turns the stance into a defined problem
          5. Possible solutions: what you will actually proposeModule 4 pressure-tests it for feasibility; Module 2 delivers it
          Nothing on this spine is optional. Your first speech under the Speakers List must carry two of these five aloud: your Point of View on the Agenda, and your Solution on the Agenda.

          Day 1 · Precursor PDF p.2

          Precursor for the Conference

          Three definitions every later rule assumes. Say them out loud with the examples.

          1. Portfolio: Country / Character / Company For example: Australia / Harry Potter / Google.
          2. Committee: Organisation that you represent your Portfolio in For example: WHO / Harry Potter / Internet Association.
          3. Agenda: Topic that is discussed across the 2 days of the Conference Verified wording: two days of the Conference (PDF p.2).
          Day 1 · Precursor PDF p.2

          Virtual Delegate Kit

          Pre-conference materials listed on PDF p.2. Day 3 research assumes delegates have opened these.

          1. Study Guide Background material for the conference preparation track.
          2. Committee Brief Committee-specific brief for the body the Portfolio sits in.
          Trainer practice · 2 min Ask every student to type in chat: their Portfolio example + their Committee example using the PDF pattern (Country/Character/Company · organisation).
          What the kit is not The Study Guide and Committee Brief tell you what the committee is about. They do not contain your portfolio's position. That is yours to research. A delegate who speaks only from the kit sounds identical to every other delegate who did the same.
          Day 1 · Key things to remember PDF p.4

          Personal pronouns, Motions, Points

          • Use of Personal Pronouns: Address yourself and everyone as “Delegate of ___” PDF: “Address yourself and everyone as ‘Delegate of ’.”
          • Motions: the request that we raise to discuss / decide something PDF definition (p.4). Full motion list appears on Day 3 (p.11).
          • Points: used to recognise yourself in the committee PDF definition (p.4). Four types on Day 2 (p.8).
          Motion or Point? The one-line test
          MotionAsks the committee to do something, and is voted on
          PointAsks the chair to recognise something, and is not voted on
          BothAre raised by a delegate, never by the Executive Board on your behalf
          The two rules that switch off, and only there Personal pronouns and electronic equipment both become permissible during an Unmoderated Caucus, and nowhere else. In every other part of the conference: third person, English, no devices.
          Day 1 · Key things to remember PDF p.4

          Representation

          • Language: Official language for all the communication is English
          • Electronic equipment is prohibited during the Formal Debate Scope is Formal Debate (p.4). Two rules become null and void in Unmoderated Caucus (p.9).
          • Attire for the Conference is either Western Formals / School Uniform
          Trainer check · 1 min Cold call: “Is a Point the same as a Motion?” Correct answer from p.4: Motions request discuss/decide; Points recognise yourself in committee.
          Three representation rules, one purpose
          LanguageEnglish is the official language for all communication
          DevicesElectronic equipment is prohibited during Formal Debate
          AttireWestern Formals or School Uniform
          Why the device rule exists In Formal Debate you are meant to be arguing from research you already did, not searching mid-speech. That is also why Point of Information requires you to name your source from memory, and why devices come back during Unmoderated Caucus, which is explicitly for research, lobbying, forming blocks and drafting.
          Day 1 · Rules regarding Debate PDF p.5

          Quorum

          • Quorum: Minimum delegates required = 1/5th of the Total Committee Size Verified formula only (PDF p.5). Do live arithmetic with the cohort’s actual size.
          Trainer practice · 2 min Pick a size (example only): if total committee = 40, quorum = 40 × 1/5 = 8. Ask two more sizes from the room. The formula is the rule; the numbers are practice.
          Presence is not agreement: three different numbers
          Quorum · 1/5thOf the Total Committee Size. About who is present.
          Simple Majority · 50% + 1Sub-topics, Unmod, Working Papers, Normal Amendments. About who agrees.
          Super Majority · 2/3rd or 67%Resolutions only.
          Why a quorum rule exists at all A decision taken by a near-empty room binds everyone who was absent. Every deliberative body from the UN General Assembly downwards therefore sets a floor before business can begin. 1/5th is this conference's floor.
          Day 1 · Rules regarding Debate PDF p.5

          Setting an Agenda & Speakers List

          1. Setting an Agenda - 1st Motion to be raised in the Conference This Motion is a formality to ensure the official announcement and declaration of the Agenda at the Conference, as the Agenda is given to all the delegates prior to the conference.
          2. Speakers List - 1st Speech of the Conference; mandatory for all the Delegates Functions in alphabetical order (A–Z or Z–A). Gets 90 seconds to speak.
          The opening sequence, in order 1. Quorum is established at 1/5th of the Total Committee Size. 2. Motion to set the Agenda: the first Motion of the conference, and a formality, because the Agenda was given to delegates prior to the conference. 3. The Speakers List opens: alphabetical, A–Z or Z–A, 90 seconds each, mandatory for every delegate. Nothing else can happen before these three.
          Day 1 · Speakers List speech PDF p.5

          Two aspects that must be spoken

          PDF p.5: two important aspects to be spoken in the Speakers List speech.

          1. Portfolio’s Point of View (POV) on the “Agenda”
          2. Solution on the “Agenda”
          Trainer practice · 3 min One volunteer: 45 seconds only (half of 90). Must include both (1) POV and (2) Solution. Cohort marks whether both appeared.
          The same two aspects appear twice On the Speakers List: POV and Solution on the Agenda. In a Moderated Caucus: POV and Solution on the Sub-Topic. Same structure, narrower scope. Learn one shape and reuse it for the whole conference.
          Day 1 · Yields PDF p.6

          Yields (1–2 of 4)

          Used at the end of the Speaker’s List if the time is remaining. Four ways to Yield (PDF p.6).

          1. Yield to Another Delegate Only applicable if the Delegate has 15 seconds or more. Remaining time can be passed to any delegate in the same committee.
          2. Yield to Questions 2 Delegates get an opportunity to ask questions with 2 Follow ups. It is mandatory to answer the question (either verbally or via Chit).
          Read "mandatory" carefully Under Yield to Questions, answering is mandatory. You choose the channel: verbally or via chit, but not whether to respond. Contrast Yield to Comments, where replying is explicitly not mandatory. This asymmetry is the most commonly missed line on page 6.
          Day 1 · Yields + recap PDF p.6

          Yields (3–4) & Day 1 close

          1. Yield to Comments 2 Delegates get an opportunity to comment for 30 seconds on the speech given by the Delegate. It is not mandatory to reply on the comment.
          2. Yield to the Chair Used when the speaker’s time is elapsed. Chairperson may utilize the time either by taking Questions or by Comments.
          Day 1 recap (verified only): Portfolio / Committee / Agenda / Kit (p.2) · “Delegate of ___”, Motions, Points, English, no electronics in Formal Debate, attire (p.4) · Quorum 1/5, Agenda formality, Speakers List 90s with POV + Solution (p.5) · four Yields (p.6).

          Day 2 · Moderated Caucus PDF p.7

          Moderated Caucus: rules

          Limited amount of time to discuss the Sub-Topic (PDF p.7).

          • Maximum time 20 mins
          • Can be started by any delegate in the committee
          • It is Voluntary to speak in Moderated Caucus
          • Flow for the Speaker in Caucus is decided by the Chairperson
          • Sub-Topic is decided by Simple Majority (50% + 1)
          • Delegates cannot yield the time
          • Delegate whose Motion is accepted / passed can either speak first or last
          Moderated Caucus at a glance
          20 minsMaximum time
          Any delegateCan start it
          VoluntarySpeaking is not compulsory, unlike the Speakers List
          50% + 1Simple Majority decides the Sub-Topic
          ChairpersonDecides the flow of speakers
          No yieldsDelegates cannot yield the time
          First or lastWhoever's Motion passed chooses their slot
          Day 2 · Moderated Caucus PDF p.7

          Raising the Motion & speech content

          • 3 important things to mention while raising a Motion: Sub Topic · Total Time · Time / Speaker
          • 2 important aspects to be spoken in the speech: (1) Portfolio’s Point of View (POV) on the “Sub-Topic” · (2) Solution on the “Sub-Topic”
          Trainer practice · 3 min Student raises a Motion aloud with all three parts. Incomplete Motion = stop and restate. Optional: 30-second Sub-Topic speech with POV + Solution.
          Day 2 · Points PDF p.8

          Points (1–2 of 4)

          Used to recognize the Delegate. Four types of Points (PDF p.8).

          1. Point of Personal Privilege Only point that can interrupt the speaker. Used when one faces any kind of discomfort and wishes to be excused.
          2. Point of Parliamentary Inquiry Used when a delegate wants to know anything about the procedure, or have any queries regarding the debate from the Executive Board.
          The interruption test Of all four Points, only Point of Personal Privilege can interrupt a delegate who is speaking. Parliamentary Inquiry, Order and Information all wait for the speaker to finish. Raising one of those mid-speech is itself a procedural error, and invites a Point of Order against you.
          Day 2 · Points PDF p.8

          Points (3–4 of 4)

          1. Point of Order Used to point out the Procedural Inconsistency or deviation from the existing rules of procedure.
          2. Point of Information Used to point Factual Inaccuracy. Have to prove the information by stating the source of information. Wikipedia, Quora & Chat GPT prohibited.
          Trainer check · 2 min Four scenarios; students name the Point. Only Personal Privilege may interrupt (p.8). Information requires a cited source; three sources banned by name.
          Day 2 · Unmoderated Caucus PDF p.9

          Unmoderated Caucus

          Break from the Formal Debate (PDF p.9).

          How it runs
          • Maximum time 20 mins
          • Can be started by any delegate in the committee
          • Motion is passed by Simple Majority (50% + 1)
          Used for 4 important aspects
          • Research
          • Lobbying
          • Formation of Blocks
          • Drafting Documents
          2 important rules get null and void (PDF p.9): Delegates can use their Electronic Equipment · Delegate can use Personal Pronouns.

          The two caucuses, side by side
          ModeratedUnmoderated
          Max time20 mins20 mins

          Day 3 · Documents PDF p.10

          Working Paper & Resolution

          Working Paper
          • Solution to the Subtopic
          • Has no format
          • Passed by Simple Majority (50% + 1)
          • Requires no Signatories
          • If passed, should be incorporated in Resolution
          Resolution
          • Solution to the Main Agenda
          • Has a Particular Format
          • Passed by Super Majority: 2/3rd or 67%
          • Requires Signatories: 1 Author; 3 Signatories (Supporting Delegates)
          • If more than 1 DRs, one with more signatories shall be discussed first
          • To be voted via Formal Voting
          Day 3 · Amendments PDF p.11

          Amendments

          Changes in the documents. Two types of Amendments (PDF p.11).

          1. Friendly Amendment Any kind of Punctuation Error or Spelling Mistake which doesn’t require a Majority.
          2. Normal Amendment Adding, Removing or Changing a clause from the Document which requires Simple Majority of 50% + 1.
          Sort these before the session: Friendly or Normal?
          FriendlyA misspelled country name
          FriendlyA missing comma in a list of clauses
          NormalChanging "urges" to "requires"
          NormalDeleting an operative clause
          NormalAdding a new obligation
          The test in one question Does the change alter what the clause obliges anyone to do? If no, it is Friendly and needs no majority. If yes, it is Normal and needs Simple Majority, 50% + 1.
          Day 3 · Types of Motions PDF p.11

          Types of Motions

          Full list from PDF p.11. Every procedural request on the floor maps to one of these.

          1. Motion to set the Agenda
          2. Motion to Adjourn the Formal Debate
          3. Motion to Suspend the Formal Debate
          4. Motion to start an Unmoderated Caucus
          5. Motion to start a Moderated Caucus
          6. Motion to Introduce Draft Resolution / Working Paper / Amendment
          7. Motion for Formal Voting
          Group them by what they do
          OpenMotion to set the Agenda
          Change the modeStart a Moderated Caucus · start an Unmoderated Caucus
          Put text on the floorIntroduce Draft Resolution / Working Paper / Amendment
          DecideMotion for Formal Voting
          StopSuspend the Formal Debate · Adjourn the Formal Debate
          Day 3 · Formal Debate formats PDF p.12

          Formats that don’t require majority

          Types of Formal Debate which don’t require majority (PDF p.12).

          1. Challenge A delegate can challenge another delegate over a particular issue for a specified period of time; this may be over a particular sub-topic or country policy. This is one on one debate.
          2. Question Answer Session Many delegates need to ask questions to a delegate. Any delegate may call for the same and committee can ask a maximum of up to 10 questions to that delegate.
          3. One for One Against When the committee usually cannot decide on a particular issue and before the final vote needs to hear both sides of the argument.
          Pick the right instrument Challenge when one delegate's position is the problem: it is one on one. Question Answer Session when many delegates need answers from one, up to 10 questions maximum. One for One Against when the committee itself is deadlocked and both sides must be heard before the final vote. None of the three requires a majority.

          Key points to Research

          Point 1 on page 3 reads "Country / Company Profile". The Guide already anticipates a corporate portfolio. Both tracks are set out together here; Module 6 works the company column in full.

          Same analysis, different comparators

          A stance only means something relative to somebody. The Guide names three comparator sets for a country; the company track names three of its own.

          Country · PEST against PDF p.3

          • BRICS Nations
          • Nations directly involved in the Agenda

          Sovereignty →Shareholder value, market share, regulatory freedom, brand

          The one rule that does not change Whichever track you are on, Possible Solutions must be traceable. A country delegate invents a policy the country never held; a company delegate invents a stance the company never took. The second is checkable in seconds by any delegate with the 10-K open.

          Module two Communication.pdf · p.1–5
          02

          Effective Communication

          You get ninety seconds on the Speakers List. Everything you researched arrives, or fails to arrive, through this module.

          Two-way streetVerbalNon-verbalListeningFour skillsLadder of InferenceSoft skillsIn committeeSDG topicsPresentation brief
          What is communication Comm p.2

          It is a two-way street

          Communication is expressing thoughts with words or actions. The definition contains a receiver, which is why sending alone is never enough.

          Verbal communication
          • Oral communication
          • Written communication
          Non-verbal communication
          • Personal appearance · Handshake
          • Body language · Clothing
          • Kinesics · Eye contact
          • Face & voice · Posture & gesture
          • Listening skills
          Why "two-way" is the whole point in committee. A speech that ignores what the previous delegate said reads as a prepared statement, not a debate contribution. The Yield to Comments and Yield to Questions rules exist precisely to force the return leg of the street.
          2 channelsVerbal and non-verbal, always running at the same time
          9 non-verbalSignals the source lists, from handshake to listening itself
          3 mentionsListening appears three separate times in this five-page source
          Verbal · oral Comm p.2 Added

          Speaking so the room can follow you

          Oral communication in committee is heard once, in real time, with no scrollback. Structure carries more weight than vocabulary.

          Structure
          • Signpost firstSay what you will cover before you cover it. The chair and the room can then track you.
          • One idea per sentenceSubordinate clauses are for writing. Spoken argument fragments under them.
          • Land the claim before the evidenceClaim, then source, then implication. Reversing this loses listeners mid-way.
          • Close on the askEnd with the solution you want the committee to act on, not with a summary.
          Delivery
          • PaceRoughly 130–150 words per minute is comfortable to follow. Ninety seconds is therefore about 200–220 words. Write to that count.
          • Pause instead of fillingA silent half-second reads as command. "Um" reads as searching.
          • Vary pitch on the claimMonotone flattens the sentence that mattered most.
          • Finish sentences down, not upRising terminals turn assertions into questions.
          The arithmetic of ninety seconds
          130–150Words per minute that a listener can comfortably follow
          200–220Words that therefore fit in your 90 seconds
          ~2Substantive claims that fit alongside a POV and a Solution
          15 secMinimum remaining time to Yield to Another Delegate
          Verbal · written Comm p.2 Added

          Written communication in committee

          Written work is read by people who did not hear your speech and who can re-read you. Precision beats persuasion here.

          What you will actually write
          • ChitsThe written channel during formal debate. Also the permitted way to answer a question under Yield to Questions.
          • Working PaperSolution to the sub-topic. Has no format, so clarity is entirely on you.
          • Draft ResolutionSolution to the main agenda. Has a particular format, and is voted on.
          • AmendmentsAdding, removing or changing a clause. Written so the change is unambiguous.
          Discipline
          • One clause, one obligationA clause that does two things invites two objections and passes neither.
          • Name the actor"Urges member states to…" beats "It is urged that…". Passive drafting hides who must act.
          • Quantify where you canA timeframe or threshold makes the clause testable. Unfalsifiable clauses get amended away.
          • Spell-check before submissionA Friendly Amendment costs the committee time on a mistake you could have caught.
          Non-verbal communication Comm p.2 Added

          Nine channels you are broadcasting on anyway

          The source lists nine non-verbal channels. Each is running whether you manage it or not, and each has a specific committee reading.

          ChannelWhat the room reads from it
          Personal appearanceWhether you treated the committee as a formal proceeding
          ClothingAttire is Western Formals or School Uniform. Deviation is noticed before you speak.
          HandshakeThe lobbying signal during unmoderated caucus. Firm, brief, eye contact.
          Body languageOpenness or defensiveness while another delegate is challenging you
          KinesicsMeaning carried by movement itself: nodding, leaning in, turning away
          Eye contactAddress the chair and the committee, not your notes. Reading down is the commonest tell.
          Face & voiceWhether your delivery matches your claim. Mismatch reads as insincerity.
          Posture & gestureStillness reads as control; fidgeting reads as unpreparedness
          Listening skillsVisible attention during others' speeches is itself a non-verbal statement
          Trainer practice On a virtual committee, most of these collapse into a webcam frame. Fix the frame once: camera at eye level, face lit from the front, upper chest and shoulders visible so gesture reads.
          Listening skills Comm p.2–3 Added

          Listening is the half most delegates skip

          The source names listening twice: once as a non-verbal channel, once among the skills you must possess, and again among the most valued soft skills. It is the most repeated item in the document.

          Levels of listening
          1. IgnoringDrafting your own speech while another delegate talks
          2. Pretend listeningNodding without processing. Exposed the moment you are asked to respond.
          3. Selective listeningHearing only the part you already planned to rebut
          4. Attentive listeningFollowing the argument as given, including the parts you dislike
          5. Empathic listeningUnderstanding why that portfolio holds that position. This is what makes lobbying work.
          What to capture while listening
          • Their claim: in one line, in their words
          • Their evidence, and whether they named a source
          • Their ask: what they want the committee to do
          • The gap: what they did not address
          • The overlap: where your solution and theirs could merge into one Working Paper
          Point of Information requires you to prove a factual inaccuracy by stating your source. You cannot raise it if you were not listening closely enough to catch the inaccuracy.
          Important skills one should possess Comm p.3 Added

          Four skills, each with a committee test

          1. Listening skillsTest: after a Moderated Caucus, can you state each speaker's position without your notes?
          2. Writing skillsTest: can a delegate who missed your speech read your clause and know exactly what to do?
          3. Presentation skillsTest: can you hold ninety seconds without reading, and land POV plus Solution inside it?
          4. Personal skillsTest: can you disagree with a delegate's position in formal debate and still lobby with them in unmoderated caucus?
          Trainer practice Run each test as a two-minute drill. The four together are the fastest diagnostic of where a delegate will actually lose points.
          Which one to fix first In a committee setting these fail in a predictable order. Listening fails first, because it is invisible and feels optional. Presentation fails next, under time pressure. Writing fails at the drafting stage, when a clause has to survive being read by a stranger. Personal skills fail last, and only under challenge. Train them in that order.
          Ladder of Inference Comm p.3 Chris Argyris

          How observation becomes belief without you noticing

          The Ladder of Inference, developed by Chris Argyris and later popularised by Peter Senge, describes the rungs we climb from raw data to action. We climb fast and rarely check.

          1. Observable dataEverything actually said or done
          2. Selected dataThe fraction you paid attention to
          3. Added meaningThe reading you place on it
          4. AssumptionsWhat you take as given based on that meaning
          5. ConclusionsWhat you decide is true
          6. BeliefsWhat you now hold about the world
          7. ActionsWhat you do, which shapes what you next observe
          The reflexive loop. Your beliefs decide which data you select next time, so the ladder feeds itself. In committee this is how a delegate becomes certain a bloc is hostile on the strength of one unanswered chit.
          Ladder of Inference · applied Added

          Climbing back down the ladder

          The value of the model is not knowing the rungs. It is having a question for each one when a debate stalls.

          RungQuestion to ask yourself, or the room
          ActionsWhat am I about to do, and what is it based on?
          BeliefsWould I have held this before this committee started?
          ConclusionsWhat would have to be true for the opposite conclusion to hold?
          AssumptionsAm I treating my portfolio's interest as a fact about the world?
          Added meaningIs this the only reading of what they said, or the most convenient one?
          Selected dataWhat did they say that I skipped past?
          Observable dataWhat are their exact words? Can I quote them back?
          Quoting a delegate back to them accurately is the single most effective move in a Challenge. It forces the debate down to observable data, where sources decide the outcome.
          Most valued soft skills in the 21st century Comm p.3

          Four, and why each is hard

          Confidence
          • Comes from preparation, not from temperament
          • Visible as stillness, eye contact, and finishing sentences
          • Its failure mode is bluffing a source you cannot name
          Positive attitude
          • Staying constructive when your clause is amended out
          • Treating a hostile question as an opening, not an attack
          • Its failure mode is conceding the room to whoever is loudest
          Good listening skills
          • The prerequisite for lobbying and for merging papers
          • The only way to catch a factual inaccuracy live
          • Its failure mode is rehearsing while others speak
          Communication skills
          • Everything above, delivered inside ninety seconds
          • Verbal and non-verbal channels agreeing with each other
          • Its failure mode is a well-researched point nobody could follow
          Applied · the Speakers List speech ROP p.5 Added

          Ninety seconds, two mandatory aspects

          The rule is fixed: your Speakers List speech gets 90 seconds and must carry your Portfolio's Point of View on the Agenda and your Solution on the Agenda. Here is a structure that fits both.

          SecondsBeatContent
          0–10Address"Delegate of [portfolio]". Establish who is speaking and to whom
          10–30POVYour portfolio's position on the agenda, stated as a claim, not a summary of the agenda
          30–55GroundingWhy that position follows from your portfolio's interests and record. Name one source.
          55–80SolutionWhat you propose the committee do. Specific enough to become a clause.
          80–90CloseRestate the ask in one line, then yield
          If time remains, you must yield. Yield to Another Delegate needs 15 seconds or more. Yield to Questions gives 2 delegates a question each with 2 follow-ups and answering is mandatory. Yield to Comments gives 2 delegates 30 seconds each and you need not reply. Yield to the Chair when your time has elapsed.
          Write it, time it, then cut it Draft to 200–220 words, read it aloud against a clock, then cut the sentence you like most that is doing the least work. Nearly every over-length first draft loses its Solution to the clock, which is the one half of the requirement the rules will not let you drop.

          Each team discusses one SDG

          Assigned topics for the communication exercise, exactly as listed in the source.

          1. SDG 1: No Poverty
          2. SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being
          3. SDG 4: Quality Education
          4. SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation
          5. SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy
          1. SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure
          2. SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities

          Same ten appear in Module 4 This list is identical to the Entrepreneurship & Innovation topic list. If your team holds the same SDG in both, treat it as one problem approached twice: Module 2 asks how you communicate it, Module 4 asks what you would build for it.
          Before you pick an angle, answer these
          WhoWhich specific group is affected, not "people"
          WhereWhich region or setting: urban, rural, coastal
          NowWhat is already being done, and by whom
          GapWhat that existing effort does not reach
          Key points for presentation Comm p.5

          Eight questions your presentation must answer

          1. What is the key message of your SDG?
          2. Who is your target audience?
          3. What are the challenges in communicating your SDG?
          4. How can good communication help the world achieve your SDG?
          5. What tools or ways (posters, videos, speeches) can you use to share your SDG message?
          6. How can you make your SDG message simple and clear for everyone to understand?
          7. Why is it important to listen to others when talking about SDGs?

          Trainer practice Question 8 asks for a real campaign. Hold teams to a named, checkable campaign with an organisation behind it. An invented example fails the same standard as an invented policy in committee.
          Module 2 recap Trainer plan

          Communication · what to carry out

          DefinitionA two-way streetExpressing thoughts with words or actions. The receiver is in the definition, so sending alone is never enough.
          ChannelsVerbal and non-verbalVerbal splits into oral and written. Nine non-verbal channels run whether you manage them or not.

          Module three Design Thinking.pdf · p.1–5
          03

          Design Thinking

          A committee agenda arrives as a topic, not a problem. This module is how you turn one into the other, and then into a solution you can defend.

          DefinitionFive phasesEmpathiseDefineIdeatePrototypeTestGroup challengesDiscussion brief
          What is Design Thinking DT p.2

          An iterative process, and a solution-based approach

          • It is iterative. We seek to understand the user, challenge assumptions, and redefine problems in an attempt to identify alternative strategies and solutions.Solutions that might not be instantly apparent with our initial level of understanding.
          • It is solution-based. Design Thinking provides a solution-based approach to solving problems.
          • It is both a mindset and a method. It is a way of thinking and working, as well as a collection of hands-on methods.
          Read the definition again for the phrase "challenge assumptions". That is the same move as climbing down the Ladder of Inference in Module 2. Design Thinking is the structured version of it.
          Four claims in the definition, each doing work
          IterativeYou will revisit phases, not pass through them once
          User-centredUnderstanding comes before solving
          Assumption-challengingIncluding your own portfolio's
          Solution-basedThe output is an answer, not a diagnosis
          Where the five-phase model comes from The Empathise–Define–Ideate–Prototype–Test formulation is the model taught by the Hasso Plattner Institute of Design at Stanford, commonly called the d.school. It is a teaching frame, not a law: other organisations describe the same work in three phases or six.
          Solution-based, not problem-based DT p.2 Added

          Why the distinction matters in committee

          Both approaches are legitimate. They produce very different speeches.

          Problem-based
          • Starts by fully characterising the obstacle
          • Asks: what exactly is wrong, and why
          • Produces analysis
          • In committee: an accurate diagnosis of the agenda that proposes nothing. The chair has heard it four times already.
          Solution-based
          • Starts from a desired outcome and works back
          • Asks: what would a working answer look like
          • Produces options to test
          • In committee: a Working Paper. The Rules of Procedure require a Solution on the Agenda in your very first speech.
          The rules are already solution-based. Speakers List speech: POV plus Solution. Moderated Caucus speech: POV plus Solution on the Sub-Topic. Working Paper: solution to the sub-topic. Resolution: solution to the main agenda. Every document in the committee is an answer, not a description.
          Phases of Design Thinking DT p.3

          Five phases

          The phases are not a queue. The process is iterative: testing sends you back to define, and defining sends you back to empathise. Expect to move backwards at least once.
          What each phase produces
          EmpathiseObservations about real people
          DefineOne problem statement
          IdeateOptions, then a selection
          PrototypeSomething concrete to react to
          TestA named failed assumption
          Phase 1 · Empathise DT p.3 Added

          Understand the user, not your idea of the user

          Empathise means setting aside your assumptions to gain insight into the people affected. In a committee context, your user is whoever the agenda actually lands on.

          Methods
          • ObserveWhat people do, which often differs from what they say they do
          • EngageAsk open questions. "Tell me about the last time…" beats "Do you find X difficult?"
          • ImmerseExperience the constraint yourself where you safely can
          • Read the recordTestimony, reports and first-hand accounts stand in for access you do not have
          In committee
          • Name the affected population precisely"Rural households without piped supply" not "people in developing countries"
          • Separate them from your portfolioYour portfolio's interest and your user's need are not the same thing. Know where they diverge before an opponent finds it.
          • Source the needAn empathy claim with no source is challengeable under Point of Information
          Phase 2 · Define DT p.3 Added

          Turn observations into one stated problem

          Define converts what you gathered into a problem statement you can actually solve. The source asks for three things: your users' needs, their problem, and your insights.

          Point-of-view statement
          [User] needs a way to [need] because [insight].
          • The need is a verb, not a solution"needs a way to store water safely", not "needs a water tank"
          • The insight is the surprising partIf the "because" clause is obvious, you have not defined anything yet
          How Might We
          • Reframe the point of view as an opening question"How might we…" is deliberately open: it presumes a solution exists without naming it
          • Too broad gives no traction"How might we end poverty?"
          • Too narrow smuggles the answer in"How might we build cheaper tanks?"
          • Right-sized constrains without decidingThe eight challenges on the next slide are written in exactly this form
          Phase 3 · Ideate DT p.3 Added

          Challenge assumptions and generate options

          The source is explicit that ideation works by challenging assumptions. Generating volume is the mechanism; challenging assumptions is the purpose.

          Diverge first
          • Separate generating from judgingEvaluating during generation kills the unusual options first, and those are the ones you came for
          • Go for quantity before qualityThe obvious ideas surface early; the useful ones arrive after you exhaust them
          • Build on others' ideas"Yes, and" rather than "yes, but"
          • Invert the problemAsk how you would guarantee failure, then reverse each answer
          Then converge
          • ClusterGroup ideas by the mechanism they rely on, not by theme
          • Select against criteria you set beforeOtherwise you will pick the idea you liked at the start
          • Keep one wild cardThe bold option is what makes a caucus remember your bloc
          Unmoderated Caucus is your ideation slot. It runs a maximum of 20 minutes and its stated uses include lobbying, formation of blocks and drafting documents. Electronic equipment is permitted during it.
          Phase 4 · Prototype DT p.3 Added

          Start creating solutions, cheaply

          A prototype exists to be wrong in front of you rather than in front of the committee. Its only job is to make the idea concrete enough to react to.

          FidelityFormAnswers
          SketchA drawing or diagram on one pageDoes the idea hold together at all?
          StoryboardThe user's journey, frame by frameWhere does it break for the person using it?
          Paper or physical mock-upA non-working stand-in you can hand to someoneIs the interaction obvious without explanation?
          Role-playAct the service out with peopleDoes the human part work?
          Working PaperThe written solution to the sub-topic, with no fixed formatWill the committee support it as drafted?
          The Working Paper is a prototype in the procedural sense. It has no format, requires no signatories, and passes by Simple Majority. If passed, it should be incorporated in the Resolution. It is designed to be revised.
          Fidelity is a budget decision Build the cheapest thing that can still be wrong in a useful way. A sketch answers "does this hold together"; only a role-play answers "does the human part work". Spending a week on a polished prototype before you know which question you are asking is the commonest waste in this phase.
          Phase 5 · Test DT p.3 Added

          Test solutions, then go back a phase

          Testing is not approval-seeking. You are looking for the fastest possible disproof of your own solution.

          What to look for
          • Where they hesitate: confusion beats politeness as a signal
          • What they work around: the workaround is the real requirement
          • What they ignore: the parts you were proudest of, usually
          • Which assumption failed: name it explicitly before you iterate
          Where it sends you
          • Mechanism failed → back to Ideate
          • Solved the wrong problem → back to Define
          • Misread who is affected → back to Empathise
          • Held up → raise it as a Working Paper
          Trainer practice The committee tests your solution for you, for free, through Challenge, Question Answer Session and One for One Against. Treat the first hostile question as data, not as an attack.
          Design Thinking with SDGs DT p.4

          Group challenges · 1 to 4

          Each challenge is stated as a How Might We question. That is deliberate.

          Group 1 · SDG 1: No Poverty
          • How might we create innovative ways to provide affordable housing for underprivileged families?
          Group 2 · SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being
          • How might we design a solution to promote mental health awareness among teenagers?
          Group 3 · SDG 5: Gender Equality
          • How might we ensure equal access to education and technology for girls in rural areas?
          Group 4 · SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities
          • How might we design eco-friendly transportation options to reduce traffic congestion in urban areas?
          Read the wording Every challenge opens with "How might we". That is a Define-phase device: it asserts a solution exists without naming it, so the group cannot skip straight to their favourite answer. Resist rewriting the challenge into a solution before you have run Empathise.
          Design Thinking with SDGs DT p.4

          Group challenges · 5 to 8

          Group 5 · SDG 14: Life Below Water
          • How might we reduce plastic waste in oceans through community-driven initiatives?
          Group 6 · SDG 4: Quality Education
          • How might we make learning more fun and accessible for children who do not have internet or digital devices?
          Group 7 · SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation
          • How might we help rural communities get clean drinking water using low-cost and sustainable solutions?
          Group 8 · SDG 13: Climate Action
          • How might we encourage students and families to take small actions every day to fight climate change?
          Each of these hides a user you have not met Before ideating: who exactly is the plastic-waste initiative asking to change behaviour, and what does their week look like? Which children lack devices, and what do they currently learn with? Named users produce specific solutions; unnamed users produce slogans.
          Design Thinking with SDG 12 DT p.5 Added mapping

          Six contents to cover in the discussion

          The six required contents map onto the five phases. Use the mapping to check you have not skipped a phase.

          ContentPhase it evidencesThe test
          a. IntroductionEmpathise + DefineWho is affected, and what is the stated problem?
          b. Brainstormed IdeasIdeate: divergeDid you generate beyond the first obvious answer?
          c. Selected IdeasIdeate: convergeOn what criteria, decided when?
          d. Plan of ActionPrototypeWho does what, and what would it cost?
          e. Benefits & ImpactTestImpact on whom, measured how?
          f. Challenges & SolutionTest: iterateWhat failed, and what did you change?
          Section f is where marks are won. A presentation with no challenges listed has either not tested the idea or is hiding the result. Both read the same way to an examiner.
          Module 3 recap Trainer plan

          Design Thinking · what to carry out

          DefinitionIterative and solution-basedUnderstand the user, challenge assumptions, redefine problems. A way of thinking and a set of hands-on methods.
          Five phasesEmpathise · Define · Ideate · Prototype · TestNot a queue. Testing sends you back to Define; defining sends you back to Empathise.
          DefinePOV statement, then How Might We[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight]. Need is a verb, never a solution.
          IdeateDiverge, then convergeSeparate generating from judging. Set selection criteria before you generate, not after.
          PrototypeBe wrong cheaplyThe Working Paper is a prototype in the procedural sense: no format, no signatories, designed to be revised.
          TestSeek disproof, not approvalWhere they hesitate, what they work around, what they ignore. Then name the assumption that failed.
          Self-test before you move on
          • Q1Write a POV statement for your group's challenge, with the need as a verb.
          • Q2Your test fails because you solved the wrong problem. Which phase do you return to?Define
          • Q3Which of the six required presentation contents is where marks are won?f. Challenges & Solution. No challenges listed means untested or hidden
          Module four Entrepreneurship & Innovation.pdf · p.1–6
          04

          Entrepreneurship & Innovation

          Module 3 produced a solution. This module asks the question that decides whether it survives contact with the world: could anyone actually build and sustain it?

          EntrepreneurshipInnovationWhy it mattersTypesThree lensesIdea to ventureProject briefSDG topicsPresentation brief
          What is Entrepreneurship E&I p.2

          Forming a new enterprise where growth is possible

          • The practice of forming a new business or commercial enterpriseUsually in an industry or sector of the economy with a large capacity for growth
          • ResourcefulnessEntrepreneurship is generally synonymous with resourcefulness
          • IngenuityAnd with ingenuity
          • Calculated riskThe ability to take calculated risks in order to introduce a new, untested product or service into the marketplace
          Note the word "calculated". The definition does not say risk-taking. It says calculated risk: the risk is priced before it is taken. That distinction is what an examiner and a hostile delegate will both probe.
          "Large capacity for growth" is part of the definition The source does not define entrepreneurship as starting any business. It specifies a sector with a large capacity for growth, and a product or service that is new and untested. Both conditions matter when you argue that your project qualifies.
          What is Innovation E&I p.3

          Renewing a domain, product or service to create new value

          • The process by which a domain, a product or a service is renewed and brought up to date
          • The meansBy applying new processes, introducing new techniques, or establishing successful ideas, to create new value
          Innovation ends in "new value", not in "new thing". Novelty that creates no value is not innovation under this definition. That is the standard your project will be judged against.
          Trainer practice Ask each team to finish the sentence "this creates value for ___ because ___" before they present. Teams that cannot fill both blanks have a novelty, not an innovation.
          Three routes the definition names
          New processesDoing the same thing a different way
          New techniquesNew capability applied to the work
          Established ideasSomething already proven, brought somewhere it was not
          The third route is the underrated one "Establishing successful ideas" means an approach that already works elsewhere counts as innovation when brought into a domain that lacks it. Your project does not have to be unprecedented. It has to create new value here.
          Innovation is crucial to us E&I p.3

          It starts as a shift in mind-set

          The source is specific about the direction of travel: innovation flows from shifts in mind-set. The mind-set comes first, the output second.

          • Shifts in mind-set generate new business models
          • They recognise new opportunities
          • They weave innovations throughout the fabric of society
          • It is about new ways of doing and seeing things as much as it is about the breakthrough idea
          "As much as it is about the breakthrough idea." This is the line that lets a modest, well-executed project beat a spectacular one. You do not need a breakthrough. You need a genuinely different way of doing or seeing.
          Three things a mind-set shift generates, per the source
          New business modelsHow the thing sustains itself
          New opportunitiesRecognised, not invented
          Innovations woven through societyNot confined to a product
          Types of innovation Added · named frameworks

          Four kinds, four different arguments

          Knowing which kind you are proposing tells you who will resist it and why.

          TypeWhat changesWho resists it
          IncrementalAn existing product or process gets measurably betterFew. Easiest to fund, hardest to differentiate.
          SustainingImproves performance for existing, usually demanding, customersNobody, which is why incumbents are good at it
          DisruptiveStarts cheaper or simpler, serves an overlooked segment, then moves upIncumbents, who rationally ignore it until it is too late
          Radical / breakthroughNew technology creating a market that did not existRegulators and existing standards bodies
          Sustaining and disruptive come from Clayton Christensen's work on why well-run incumbent firms lose to entrants. If your solution is disruptive, expect the industry association in your committee to oppose it. That is the model's prediction, and you can say so out loud.
          Why this matters in a committee of companies If your solution is sustaining, incumbents will support it, because it makes their existing offer better. If it is disruptive, expect the industry association to oppose it, because associations speak for incumbents. Naming which kind you are proposing lets you predict the room before you enter it.
          The project focus E&I p.4 Added

          Creativity, Feasibility, Impact

          The source names three criteria for the project. They correspond closely to the desirability–feasibility–viability triad used in design and venture practice.

          Creativity
          • Thinking ideas out of the box
          • Test: could another team have produced this in five minutes without research? If yes, it is not yet creative.
          • Related lens: desirability: does anyone actually want it?
          Feasibility
          • Could this idea work in real life?
          • Test: name the materials, the people and the money. Vagueness here is the commonest failure.
          • Related lens: viability: can it sustain itself past launch?
          Impact
          • How will it help people or the environment?
          • Test: impact on whom, at what scale, measured how?
          • Ties directly to the SDG you were assigned
          The project focus · missing a lens E&I p.4 Added

          Which pair you have tells you what to fix

          An idea has to clear all three criteria. The two you already hold identify the question you have not yet answered.

          What each pair alone produces
          Creative + feasible, no impactA clever thing nobody needed. Busywork.
          Creative + impactful, not feasibleA wish. It presents well and cannot be built.
          Feasible + impactful, not creativeProbably already tried. Find out by whom, and why it stalled.
          An idea has to clear all three. The pair you are missing tells you which question to go and answer next.
          From idea to venture Added · named frameworks

          Six questions between an idea and a working venture

          These map onto the presentation brief on the next slides. Answer them in this order.

          1. Problem: what specifically is broken, for whomStated as a problem, not as the absence of your solution
          2. Customer / beneficiary: who is most affected, and how it shapes their daySegment it. "Everyone" is not a segment.
          3. Value proposition: what you offer, and why it beats the current alternativeThe current alternative is usually "do nothing", which is free and therefore hard to beat
          4. Minimum viable version: the smallest build that tests the riskiest assumptionFrom Eric Ries's lean startup method: build, measure, learn
          5. Resources: materials, tools, skills, money, partnersThis is where feasibility becomes checkable
          6. Growth path: how it reaches more people if it worksDistribution is a design decision, not an afterthought
          New business models E&I p.3 Added · Osterwalder

          What a business model has to specify

          The source says shifts in mind-set "generate new business models". A business model is not the idea; it is how the idea keeps existing after launch. The Business Model Canvas, developed by Alexander Osterwalder, names the parts.

          Who you serve
          • Customer segments
          • Customer relationships
          • Channels
          What you offer
          • Value propositions
          • Key activities
          • Key resources
          • Key partners
          How it sustains
          • Revenue streams
          • Cost structure
          For an SDG project, "revenue" may be grant funding, public budget or cross-subsidy. It still has to be named. A solution with no funding mechanism is a proposal for someone else to pay, and the committee will ask who.
          The project E&I p.4

          Solve the problem, create a product, or offer a service

          Aligned with the SDG assigned to your team.

          Focus on
          • Creativity: thinking ideas out of the box
          • Feasibility: could this idea work in real life?
          • Impact: how will it help people or the environment?
          SDGs named for the project
          • SDG 2: Zero Hunger
          • SDG 4: Quality Education
          • SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation
          • SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy
          • SDG 13: Climate Action
          Five SDGs here, ten on the next slide The project brief names five SDGs; the discussion list names ten. Where they differ, the project brief governs what you build and the discussion list governs what your team debates. Check which one your assignment came from before you start.

          Eight questions your project must answer

          1. What is the problem your team is trying to solve related to your SDG?
          2. Who is most affected by this problem, and how does it impact their daily life?
          3. What is your team's idea for a product or service that could help solve this problem?
          4. What makes your idea unique or different from what already exists?
          5. What materials or tools will you need to build or launch your idea?
          6. How will your idea help people or the planet in a simple and useful way?
          7. How will you let others know about your idea or service?
          8. If your idea is successful, how will it grow and help more people?
          They map to the three criteria Questions 1–2 establish the problem and who it lands on. Questions 3–4 are your Creativity score. Questions 5 and 7 are Feasibility. Questions 6 and 8 are Impact. An answer you cannot give is a criterion you will lose marks on.
          Answering the brief well Added

          The weak answer and the strong answer

          Every one of the eight questions has a version that sounds complete and says nothing. Here is the difference on the four that decide the result.

          QuestionWeakStrong
          Q2 · Who is affected"People in developing countries"A named segment, with what their day looks like now
          Q4 · What makes it unique"Nothing like it exists"Names two things that do exist, and the specific gap between them
          Q5 · Materials and tools"Technology and funding"An itemised list someone could go and buy
          Q8 · How it grows"We will scale it up"The next segment, the next region, and what breaks at that size
          Trainer practice Q4 is the one to press hardest. A team that claims nothing comparable exists has almost always not looked. Two minutes of searching usually finds a comparable, and finding it yourself is far better than an examiner finding it.
          Module 4 recap Trainer plan

          Entrepreneurship & Innovation · what to carry out

          EntrepreneurshipCalculated risk, not riskForming a new enterprise where growth is possible. Resourcefulness, ingenuity, and risk that is priced before it is taken.
          InnovationEnds in new valueRenewing a domain, product or service by new processes, techniques or established ideas. Novelty without value does not qualify.
          Mind-set first"As much as the breakthrough idea"New ways of doing and seeing count equally. A modest, well-executed project can beat a spectacular one.
          Three criteriaCreativity · Feasibility · ImpactAll three, or it fails. Creative but infeasible is a wish; feasible but low-impact is busywork.
          TypesIncremental · Sustaining · Disruptive · RadicalKnowing which you propose tells you who will oppose it, and why.
          ModelName the funding mechanismGrant, public budget or cross-subsidy, but named. A solution with no funding is a proposal for someone else to pay.
          Self-test before you move on
          • Q1Finish this sentence for your project: "this creates value for ___ because ___".
          • Q2Name two things that already exist in your problem space, and the gap between them.This is the strong answer to "what makes your idea unique"
          • Q3Your solution is disruptive. Who does Christensen's model predict will oppose it?The incumbents, and the industry association that speaks for them
          Module five Major Events that Changes the World.pdf · p.1–3
          05

          Major Events That Changed the World

          The Rules of Procedure require the past of the agenda as well as its current situation. This module is where that half comes from.

          Why historyThe ten eventsThe causal chainThe seven-part frameTimelinesWhat ifWinners and losersRecap
          Why this module exists ROP p.3 Added

          Precedent is the only argument that cannot be dismissed as opinion

          • The rules require it. Research point 3 is the Agenda, split into the past of the agenda and the current situation of the agenda. Half the requirement is historical.
          • It survives Point of Information. A documented event with a stated source cannot be waved away. A prediction can.
          • It supplies the mechanism. Knowing that something happened is weak. Knowing how it happened lets you argue whether the same mechanism is present now.
          • It sets the burden of proof. If the historical case ran one way, the delegate arguing this time is different has to say what changed.
          The failure mode. Analogy without mechanism. "This is just like the Great Depression" invites the reply "in what respect?", and if you cannot name the respect, you have handed the room to your opponent.
          How a historical claim survives challenge
          DatedA year, ideally a month, that an opponent can look up
          SourcedNameable out loud, and not Wikipedia, Quora or Chat GPT
          MechanisticYou can say how it happened, not only that it did
          BoundedYou state where the analogy stops before you are asked
          Topics of discussion ME p.2

          Ten events

          1. Industrial Revolution
          2. The Great Depression
          3. World War II
          4. Cold War
          5. The birth of the Internet
          1. Google was founded
          2. COVID-19
          3. Introduction of AI

          5. Hiroshima and Nagasaki
          These ten are not independent. Six of them form one causal chain, shown on the next slide. Presenting one link without the chain loses most of its explanatory power.
          Sort them before you present

          The chain Added · documented sequence

          Six of the ten are one story

          Each arrow is a documented consequence, not a loose association. This is the spine to hang the other four events on.

          Focus on ME p.3

          The seven-part frame your slides must carry

          The source specifies what the slides of the presentation should contain. All seven, in this order.

          1. What was the event?
          2. What was the world like before this event?
          3. What happened during the event?
          4. What was the world like after this event?
          1. The "What If" scenario
          2. Impact on daily life
          3. Winners and losers / beneficiaries and sufferers
          Why this order Parts 2–4 establish what changed. Part 5 tests what caused it. Parts 6–7 establish who it landed on. Skipping straight to part 7 produces a verdict with no evidence behind it.
          Common failures, part by part
          Parts 2–4Describing "before" as merely the absence of "after"
          Part 3Listing highlights instead of the sequence and the mechanism
          Part 5Changing several things at once, which proves nothing
          Part 6Staying abstract where the question asks for daily specifics
          Part 7Presenting one side and calling it a conclusion
          Before · During · After ME p.3 Added

          Three snapshots, one comparison

          The frame only works if you hold the same variables constant across all three panels. Pick your variables first.

          Before
          • Who held power, and on what basis
          • How people earned and lived
          • What was technically possible
          • Which institutions existed
          • Resist describing "before" as simply the absence of "after"
          During
          • The trigger, and the date
          • The sequence, not just the highlights
          • Decisions that could have gone otherwise
          • Who acted, and who was acted upon
          • This panel is where the mechanism lives
          After
          • The same variables as "before", re-measured
          • Which changes stuck and which reverted
          • Institutions created or destroyed
          • What became newly thinkable
          • Separate immediate aftermath from long-run settlement
          Anchors · industrial and economic Added · documented dates

          Industrial Revolution and the Great Depression

          • c. 1760sIndustrial Revolution begins in Britain: mechanised textile production, then the factory systemMechanism: power and machinery replace hand production, concentrating work in cities
          • 1769James Watt patents his improved steam engineDecouples industry from water-mill sites; factories can be built anywhere
          • 1825Stockton and Darlington Railway opensRailways collapse the cost of moving goods; markets become national, then international
          • 1914–1918First World WarRedraws the map and leaves the international debt structure the 1920s ran on
          • Oct 1929Wall Street CrashTrigger, not sole cause. Bank failures and credit contraction turn a crash into a decade.
          • 1930sThe Great Depression: mass unemployment, trade barriers, collapse in world trade
          • 1944Bretton Woods conference: IMF and World Bank foundedThe institutional answer: never again leave the monetary system without a coordinator
          Worked example · Industrial Revolution Added · the seven-part frame applied

          The frame, filled in

          What was the eventThe shift from hand production to machine and factory production, beginning in Britain around the 1760s and spreading through Europe and North America across the next century
          BeforeMost people worked in agriculture or cottage industry, at home, at the pace of daylight and season. Power came from muscle, water and wind.
          DuringSteam power, mechanised textiles, coal, iron, then railways. Work moved into factories and people moved into cities.
          AfterUrban, industrial societies. Wage labour, the clock, the factory shift. New classes, new politics, and eventually organised labour and factory regulation.
          What ifWithout the separate condenser, steam stays inefficient and industry stays tied to water power, dispersed along rivers rather than concentrated in cities
          Daily lifeTime itself was reorganised. The working day became fixed hours set by an employer rather than by task and season.
          Winners / losersFactory owners and industrialising states gained. Handloom weavers and other skilled artisans were displaced; early factory workers, including children, bore the conditions.
          Anchors · war and world order Added · documented dates

          World War II, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the UN, the Cold War

          • 1939–1945Second World WarGlobal in scope, industrial in method, and total in the sense that civilian economies were targets
          • Feb 1945Yalta Conference: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin agree the shape of the post-war settlementIncluding the plan for a United Nations organisation and its Security Council
          • 6 & 9 Aug 1945Atomic bombing of Hiroshima and NagasakiThe only use of nuclear weapons in war. Deterrence becomes a permanent feature of world politics.
          • 26 Jun 1945UN Charter signed in San Francisco by 50 nations; Poland signed later as the 51st original member
          • 24 Oct 1945The United Nations comes into existence as the Charter enters into forceSecurity Council with five permanent members: the P5 your PEST analysis compares against
          • 1948Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the General Assembly
          • 1947–1991Cold War: bipolar order, proxy conflicts, deterrence, non-alignment
          • Dec 1991Dissolution of the Soviet UnionBipolarity ends; the 1944–1948 institutions remain, now operating in a different world
          History byte The UN was not built after the war as a reaction. Planning ran during it: the name "United Nations" was used for the wartime alliance from 1942, three years before the Charter.
          Worked example · 1945 Added · documented dates

          One year, and the order we still argue inside

          Every institution your committee resembles was designed within eighteen months of these events. Understanding the year explains the rules.

          • FebYalta: the three Allied leaders agree post-war structures
          • Apr–JunSan Francisco Conference: 50 nations negotiate the UN Charter
          • 26 JunCharter signed
          • 6 & 9 AugHiroshima and Nagasaki
          • 2 SepJapan's formal surrender: the Second World War ends
          • 24 OctUN Charter enters into force: UN Day
          51Original UN member states, including Poland which signed after the conference
          5Permanent Security Council members with veto power: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US
          1948Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted
          Anchors · networks, platforms, pandemics, AI Added · documented dates

          The Internet, Google, COVID-19, AI

          • 1956Dartmouth Summer Research Project: the term "artificial intelligence" is coinedAI is older than the internet. What changed recently is capability, not the concept.
          • 1969ARPANET's first node-to-node connectionPacket switching: no central exchange, so the network survives losing parts of itself
          • 1 Jan 1983ARPANET adopts TCP/IPA common protocol turns separate networks into one internet
          • 1989–1991Tim Berners-Lee proposes and releases the World Wide Web at CERNTurns a research network into a publishing medium anyone can use
          • 1998Google founded by Larry Page and Sergey BrinSearch becomes the organising layer; advertising becomes the model that funded the consumer web
          • 2012AlexNet wins the ImageNet competitionDeep learning on GPUs becomes the dominant approach in AI
          • 11 Mar 2020WHO characterises COVID-19 as a pandemicThe first event on this list experienced everywhere at once, in real time, over the network above
          • Nov 2022ChatGPT released publiclyMoves AI from a research and infrastructure story into a mass-consumer and regulatory one
          History byte The internet and the web are not the same event. The internet is the network (1969, then TCP/IP in 1983). The web is one application running on it (1989–1991). Delegates conflate them constantly.
          Worked example · the network era Added

          Why COVID-19 belongs on a list with the Industrial Revolution

          The argument to make. The Industrial Revolution reorganised where and when people worked. The network era reorganised whether location matters at all, and COVID-19 was the moment that shift was tested worldwide, simultaneously, because the infrastructure to work and learn remotely already existed. An identical pandemic in 1990 would have had no such option.
          The "What If" scenario ME p.3 Added

          Counterfactuals, done properly

          A "what if" is not speculation for its own sake. It is a test of which cause was actually load-bearing.

          Rules for a usable counterfactual
          • Change one thingAlter a single decision or event, then follow the consequences. Changing several at once proves nothing.
          • Keep it plausibleThe alternative must have been genuinely available to the people at the time
          • Follow the mechanism, not the moodTrace the chain: this institution never forms, so this treaty has no forum, so…
          • Stop before it becomes fictionConsequences get less knowable the further you run them. Two or three steps is honest; ten is not.
          Worked counterfactuals
          No Bretton Woods, 1944No IMF or World Bank. The 1930s pattern of competitive devaluation and trade barriers has no standing coordinator to interrupt it.
          No TCP/IP standard, 1983Networks stay incompatible. "The internet" is several national networks that cannot address each other.
          No veto in the CharterThe great powers likely do not join. A universal body without them is the League of Nations again.
          In committee: a counterfactual is the strongest form of "here is why this proposal matters". You are showing what the absence of action cost last time.
          Winners and losers · impact on daily life ME p.3 Added

          Every event on the list has both, at the same time

          The source asks for beneficiaries and sufferers. Presenting only one side is the fastest way to be challenged.

          • Split by group, not by verdictWho gained and who lost among: workers, owners, states, colonised populations, women, children, future generations. The answer usually differs by group.
          • Split by timescaleThe Industrial Revolution's immediate effect on factory workers and its century-scale effect on living standards point in opposite directions. Both are true.
          • Split by geography"The world" rarely experiences an event uniformly. Name the regions.
          • Impact on daily life is the concrete testWhat time did people get up, what did they eat, what did they fear, what could they do that they could not before? Abstractions hide here.
          • Name your own portfolio's sideIf your portfolio was a beneficiary, say so before an opponent does. Owning it costs far less than being caught.
          Trainer practice Assign each team the side their portfolio was not on and have them argue it for two minutes. It is the fastest cure for one-sided historical framing.

          Module six company-portfolio-prep-track.md
          06

          Company Portfolio Prep Track

          Same research spine as a country portfolio. What changes is the actor's interest: a company optimises for market position, regulatory freedom and shareholder value, not sovereignty or citizenry.

          Country vs companyFive research pointsPrimary sourcesFinancial dataRegulatoryCompetitiveESGPeoplePressSix stagesWorked templateChecklist
          The whole module in one question md · intro

          What would this company actually say in this room, and can you prove it from a primary source?

          Every resource in this module is chosen to answer that one question. The spine is unchanged from the country track: Portfolio → Committee → Agenda → Policy Stance → Solution.

          The failure mode is specific and checkable. A country delegate who invents a policy may not be caught. A company delegate who invents a stance can be refuted in seconds by any delegate with the 10-K open. Corporate positions are filed, dated and public.
          Four questions the module answers in order
          Who is this companyOwnership, business lines, scale (§3.1, §3.2)
          What has it been held toAntitrust, litigation, lobbying (§3.3)
          Who does it stand besideCompetitors and the association line (§3.4)
          Who argues against itNGO and watchdog reports (§3.5)
          The asymmetry to keep in mind A country's position can be genuinely ambiguous. A public company's position is filed, dated and searchable. That cuts both ways: it is harder to bluff, and far easier to prove.
          Country vs company · what changes md §1

          Seven dimensions that shift

          DimensionCountry portfolioCompany portfolio
          Core interestNational sovereignty, citizens, geopolitical standingShareholder value, market share, regulatory freedom, brand
          "Foreign policy" equivalentBilateral / multilateral relationsCompetitive strategy + regulatory posture
          PEST comparator setvs. P5, vs. BRICS, vs. nations in the agendavs. regulators in the agenda, vs. top 2–3 competitors, vs. industry association line
          Primary filingsTreaties, UN resolutions, gov policy papers10-K / Annual Report, proxy statement, ESG report
          Accountability bodyUN, State Dept, national parliamentSEC / home regulator, antitrust authority, shareholders
          "Embassy" equivalentElectronic Embassy, State Dept notesInvestor Relations page, corporate newsroom, IR contact
          Failure modeInventing a policy the country never heldInventing a stance the company never publicly took
          What does not shift The spine is unchanged: Portfolio → Committee → Agenda → Policy Stance → Possible Solutions. The 90-second speech still needs a POV and a Solution. Quorum, majorities, yields and Points are identical. Only the actor's interest and the evidence base change.
          Key points to research · retargeted md §2

          The same five points, aimed at a corporate actor

          1. Company ProfileFounding, HQ, ownership structure (public / private / state-linked / subsidiary), leadership, core business lines, scale
          2. CommitteeWhat this industry body or organisation actually regulates or coordinates, and why this company is a member
          3. AgendaPast state and current state, specifically as it affects this company's revenue, liability or market access
          4. Corporate Policy StancePESTEL analysis of your company against regulators named in the agenda, the top 2–3 competitors' public positions, and the industry association's official line
          5. Possible SolutionsMust be traceable to something the company has already said, filed or funded
          On point 5: a solution that contradicts the 10-K risk factors section will get challenged and will not survive. Read the risk factors before you draft the solution, not after.

          Zero-to-hero track · stages 0–2 md §5

          Orient, profile, map the sector

          Stage 0
          ~30 min
          Orientation: reframe from "citizen-representative" to corporate self-interestDiscuss who this company serves and what it wants out of this committee. Deliverable: a one-paragraph statement of the company's core interest in the agenda.
          Stage 1
          2–3 hrs
          Company Profile: build the factual baseFounding, HQ, ownership, leadership, business lines, scale, revenue. Pull from §3.1 and §3.2. Deliverable: a one-page Company Factsheet.
          Stage 2
          2–3 hrs
          Competitive Landscape: map the sectorIdentify the top 2–3 competitors, the industry association, and market position. Pull from §3.3 and §3.4. Deliverable: a Competitive Landscape table (competitor, position, differentiator).
          Stage 0 is not optional warm-up. Delegates who skip it argue like a country for the first two sessions, defending the public interest instead of the company's interest, and have to unlearn it.
          Stage 0 is 30 minutes and saves hours A delegate who has not made the mindset shift argues for the public interest, because that is the instinct a country portfolio trains. A company may well arrive at a public-interest position, but it gets there through market position, regulatory freedom and shareholder value, and it must be argued that way.
          Zero-to-hero track · stages 3–5 md §5

          Stance, speech, simulation

          Stage 3
          3–4 hrs
          Policy Stance (PESTEL): the core deliverable, equivalent to the country track's PEST sectionRun PESTEL against regulators in the agenda, competitors, and the industry association line; pull the adversarial NGO view for stress-testing. Deliverable: a Policy Stance Matrix (P-E-S-T-E-L rows × comparator columns).
          Stage 4
          1.5–2 hrs
          Position & Speech Draft: turn research into the 90-second Speakers List speechDraft POV on agenda plus proposed solution; verify every claim against a primary source from stages 1–3. Deliverable: a source-tagged speech draft.
          Stage 5
          ongoing
          Simulation & Crisis Readiness: battle-test the positionMock caucusing, Challenge rounds, Q&A defending the stance live; practise citing the 10-K, court filings and testimony from memory. 2–3 mock sessions before the conference.
          Total dedicated prep: roughly 10–13 hours, front-loaded before conference week, with Stage 5 repeated as mock-session slots allow.

          Pre-committee checklist md §7

          Eight boxes, all ticked before you walk in

          • Company Factsheet complete (§3.1, §3.2)
          • Top 2–3 competitors and industry association position identified (§3.3, §3.4)
          • PESTEL Policy Stance Matrix filled, cross-checked against an adversarial source (§3.5)

          • Adversarial / NGO view reviewed so hostile questions are not a surprise
          • At least one primary-source figure, financial or legal, memorised for live citation
          • Google News Alert live on the company name through conference week
          • Mock Challenge round completed at least once before the real committee
          Box 6 is the one delegates skip. Reading a figure and being able to state it live under a Point of Information are different skills. Memorise one number and its source.
          If you only have one evening Do boxes 1, 4 and 6. A Company Factsheet, a speech where every claim is source-tagged, and one primary-source figure held in memory will carry you through an opening speech and a first challenge. The rest deepens the position; those three make it defensible.

          Putting it together Trainer plan

          How the six modules meet in one speech

          Ninety seconds on the Speakers List uses all six at once. That is the point of the programme.

          ModuleWhat it contributes to those 90 seconds
          01 · Rules of ProcedureThat you get 90 seconds at all, what must be in them, and how to yield the remainder
          02 · CommunicationThe structure and delivery that make the content land, and the listening that lets you answer
          03 · Design ThinkingThe defined problem behind your POV, and the tested solution you propose
          04 · Entrepreneurship & InnovationWhether that solution is feasible, who funds it, and how it grows
          05 · Major EventsThe past of the agenda, and the precedent your argument rests on
          06 · Company PortfolioThe primary source behind every claim you make
          The single test of the whole programme: can you make a claim, name its source, propose an action, and defend all three under a Challenge?
          The order you will actually use them in Before conference: Module 6 gathers the evidence, Module 5 supplies the precedent, Module 3 defines the problem, Module 4 tests the solution. In the room: Module 1 gives you the procedure and Module 2 gives you the delivery. Research is slow and front-loaded; performance is fast and unrepeatable.
